section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department diplomatic correspondence and intelligence reports from late June through July 1941 (with one follow-up memorandum from April 1942) addressing the acute political crisis in Japan following the German invasion of the Soviet Union. The sudden German-Soviet hostilities shattered the assumptions underpinning Japan's alliance with Germany, prompting intense deliberations, the en bloc resignation of the second Konoye Cabinet on July 16, and the rapid formation of the third Konoye Cabinet under Prince Fumimaro Konoye on July 18. Diplomatic telegrams from Tokyo, Berlin, Rome, Moscow, and Shanghai analyze the strategic ouster of Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, his replacement by Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda, Tokyo's public assertions of national self-reliance, and Japanese military preparations to occupy strategic bases in southern French Indochina. Accompanying reports from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Consulate at Kobe document industrial conditions, critical raw material shortages, Japanese espionage practices, naval fleet movements, and stringent wartime port restrictions.

subfiles.about: Captain E. Jackson of the S.S. Clevendon reports on the Amagasaki electric plant, coal and food shortages in Japan, and Japanese naval intelligence operations disguised as ship repairs in Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: Captain E. Jackson tells the FBI of Amagasaki power plant conditions, rice, leather and water shortages near Kobe-Osaka, and a Hong Kong freighter used for naval intelligence.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Intelligence Furnished by Captain E. Jackson Concerning Industrial and Strategic Conditions in Japan and Hong Kong

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the convening of the Fourth Imperial Conference and statements issued by the Japanese Government and Foreign Minister Matsuoka regarding the German-Soviet war.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Fourth Imperial Conference of July 2, 1941 decided fundamental national policy. Matsuoka called the German-Soviet war a 'super emergency period' and urged unity.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 920 from Tokyo on the Fourth Imperial Conference and Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Statement

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes high-level Japanese policy debates revealing growing friction between German and Japanese conceptions of their new orders and press doubts regarding the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports German-Japanese strains: the Wohltat mission ignored Japan's dominance, Kokumin warns that the German attack on the USSR puts the Tripartite and Neutrality Pacts in conflict, threatening the alliance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 913 from Tokyo on Strains in the Tripartite Alliance and Conflicting German and Japanese Ambitions

subfiles.about: Ambassador MacMurray reports confidential warnings from former Turkish Prime Minister Rauf Bey regarding Japanese Pan-Islamic intrigues in Iraq and Central Asia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador MacMurray reports Rauf Bey's claims of Japanese pan-Islamic subversion: the Iraq revolt was Japanese-engineered, and Japanese agents sought his leadership of a Turcoman state.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ankara regarding Japanese Subversive and Pan-Islamic Activities in the Middle East and Central Asia

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reviews Tokyo newspaper editorials reacting to the July 2 Imperial Conference, emphasizing national self-reliance, unity, and resolution of the China Incident.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes press reaction to the July 2 Imperial Conference: calls for unity and sacrifice; Hochi says Japan must rely on itself; Miyako says aid to Chiang must stop, and force may be used to advance south.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 927 from Tokyo on Japanese Press Reactions to the Imperial Conference Decisions

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on Prime Minister Konoye's national radio address on East Asia Day emphasizing national perseverance, patriotism, and self-sufficiency.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Konoye's July 1 East Asia Day radio address, praising resilience through five years of conflict, promising self-sufficiency from East Asian resources and urging national unity.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 919 from Tokyo on Prime Minister Konoye's East Asia Day Radio Address

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on press commentary regarding frequent private meetings between Premier Konoye and Marquis Kido, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal.
subfiles.summary: Grew cites a Kokumin article on frequent Konoye-Kido conferences, which the press sees as possibly presaging a renovation of national policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 969 from Tokyo on Speculation Concerning Frequent Conferences Between Konoye and Kido

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew sends an urgent triple-priority telegram reporting that the entire Japanese Cabinet resigned en bloc.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports at midnight on July 16, 1941 that the entire Japanese Cabinet resigned en bloc; no details yet.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1014 from Tokyo on the Resignation of the Japanese Cabinet En Bloc

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew sends a rush telegram confirming that Prince Fumimaro Konoye will head the newly formed Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Prince Konoye will head the new Japanese Cabinet after receiving the imperial command.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1019 from Tokyo announcing Konoye to Head New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew details the conference of senior statesmen (Jushin) that recommended Konoye to form a new cabinet and the resignations of top administrative officials.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the July 17 senior statesmen conference after which the Emperor commanded Konoye to form a cabinet, and the resignations of advisory council members, vice ministers and officials.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1022 from Tokyo on the Senior Statesmen Conference and Resignations of Key Officials

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits the official statement of the Board of Information explaining the Cabinet's en bloc resignation.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits the Board of Information statement: the cabinet resigned en bloc to strengthen its internal structure; Konoye presented the resignations at Hayama, and the Emperor told him to continue.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1016 from Tokyo transmitting Board of Information Statement on Cabinet Resignation

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the ministerial lineup of the third Konoye Cabinet, including Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Grew announces the third Konoye Cabinet: Konoye is also Justice Minister, Vice Admiral Toyoda Foreign Minister, Tojo and Oikawa remain, with Hiranuma, Yanagawa and Suzuki without portfolio.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1029 from Tokyo announcing Personnel of the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a biographical sketch and diplomatic appraisal of Vice Admiral Teijiro Toyoda, the newly appointed Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Grew assesses Vice Admiral Toyoda as Foreign Minister: Navy administrator, not pro-Axis, speaks good English and is friendly toward the US and Britain.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1030 from Tokyo assessing Background and Outlook of Foreign Minister Teijiro Toyoda

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on press reactions under censorship constraints, Konoye's conferences with Hiranuma and service ministers, and the political sidelining of Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports strict censorship; Konoye conferred with Hiranuma and the service ministers, and Matsuoka has been ill and absent since July 10.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1024 from Tokyo on Cabinet Reorganization Developments and Political Maneuvers

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a confidential analysis attributing the Cabinet collapse to German-Soviet hostilities, Hiranuma's insistence on ministerial responsibility, and Konoye's desire to drop Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Grew analyzes the cabinet crisis: the German attack on the USSR undermined the German alliance, and Konoye clashed with Matsuoka over the Tripartite Pact. Resignation en bloc was a device to purge Matsuoka.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1025 from Tokyo analyzing Underlying Causes of the Cabinet Crisis and Matsuoka's Ouster

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the resignations of Ambassador to Nanking Kumataro Honda and Foreign Vice Minister Chuichi Ohashi following the cabinet shakeup.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Ambassador Honda and Vice Minister Ohashi resigned, per press, after Matsuoka's removal.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1033 from Tokyo on the Resignations of Ambassador Honda and Vice Minister Ohashi

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits public statements by Prince Konoye and War Minister Tojo affirming that national policy remains fixed and immutable while urging swift consolidation of the wartime structure.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Konoye said policy was fixed but needs speed, and Tojo said policy is unchanged and urged unity of government and military organs.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1034 from Tokyo transmitting Statements by Premier Konoye and War Minister Tojo

subfiles.about: Chargé Leland Morris reports on subdued German reactions in Berlin to the Tokyo cabinet shakeup and Germany's concern over Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Morris reports Berlin covered the Japanese cabinet change with subdued prominence, claiming Japan remains committed to the Three Power Pact; hopes for a Japanese move against Russia seem to have receded.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2901 from Berlin on German Press and Official Reactions to the Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on a national radio address by Information Board President Nobufumi Ito urging Japan to depend solely on its own strength.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Information Board chief Ito's radio address: the cabinet reorganization consolidates the home front, and Japan must rely on no other nation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1036 from Tokyo on Information Board Chief Ito's Radio Address on Self-Reliance

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports a Yomiuri editorial emphasizing that the fundamental foreign policy formulated at the Imperial Conference remains unaltered.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes a Yomiuri editorial: the July 2 Imperial Conference policy is intact, changes are of tone and method, and Japan must rely on its own strength.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1037 from Tokyo on Yomiuri Editorial on Foreign Policy Continuity and Self-Reliance

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive four-part assessment of the third Konoye Cabinet, Tokyo press reactions, the Konoye-Hiranuma axis, and the diplomatic impact of Matsuoka's removal.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 1035 (sections 1 through 4), Ambassador Grew analyzes the reception and composition of the third Konoye Cabinet. The Japanese press acclaimed its rapid formation, strong military representation, and exclusion of party politicians, viewing it as a reorganization rather than a governmental collapse. Commentators identified a dominant Konoye-Hiranuma axis, with Baron Hiranuma functioning as virtual Vice Premier, while new Foreign Minister Toyoda emphasized diplomatic flexibility rather than slavish adherence to foreign systems. Financial circles welcomed Masatsune Ogura's appointment to Finance, anticipating close cooperation with Suzuki and Sakonji. Grew concludes that Matsuoka's eclipse eliminates a pro-Nazi influence fundamentally unacceptable to Japan, providing a unified administration that is less likely to follow German dictates or precipitate a clash with the United States.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1035 from Tokyo on Political Composition and Significance of the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Consul General Lockhart summarizes Shanghai press reactions across English-language, Japanese, and Chinese newspapers concerning the new Tokyo cabinet and Matsuoka's ouster.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Lockhart summarizes Shanghai press: English papers saw Matsuoka's removal with Toyoda cautious but possibly advancing into Indochina; Japanese papers warn the West against expecting an Axis break; Chungking papers see rapprochement overtures.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 900 from Shanghai on Local Press Reactions to the Japanese Cabinet Shakeup

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew summarizes Tokyo press editorials on the need for independent diplomacy and media criticism of Foreign Office officials resigning out of loyalty to Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Grew reviews press comment: Hochi says the German-Soviet war altered Japan's diplomatic premise, Miyako wants independent diplomacy, and Kokumin and Chugai criticize Matsuoka's followers' resignations and farewell.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1043 from Tokyo reviewing Press Commentary on Foreign Policy Independence and Resignations

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits Tokyo press editorials advocating flexible diplomacy to adapt to the German-Soviet conflict while settling the China incident.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes Asahi, Miyako and Chugai: basic policy unchanged but diplomacy must be flexible after the German-Soviet war, with China the priority.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1049 from Tokyo reviewing Press Calls for Diplomatic Flexibility

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew presents an in-depth analysis of the growing Japanese estrangement from Nazi Germany, German arrogance in Tokyo, and the prospects for Japan's foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: In telegram No. 1052 (sections 1 and 2, along with its official State Department paraphrase on page 218), Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive assessment of the strategic forces behind the cabinet crisis. Grew deduces that Japan is increasingly dissatisfied with its subordinate role in the Axis alliance, noting that while the unannounced German invasion of Russia precipitated the crisis, long-term resentment had been provoked by German arrogance, racial contempt for the Japanese, intrusive Gestapo activities in Tokyo, and German Ambassador Ott's overbearing attempts to regiment the Japanese press. Baron Hiranuma forced the cabinet's resignation on the constitutional principle that ministers must accept responsibility for failing to anticipate the German attack. Grew predicts no sudden volte-face away from the Tripartite Pact, but observes that dropping Matsuoka—dismissively called 'Hitler's office boy'—enables Tokyo to pursue an independent foreign policy and could eventually lead to gradual rapprochement with Anglo-American nations.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1052 and Paraphrase from Tokyo analyzing Japanese Disillusionment with the Axis and Future Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Ambassador Phillips reports on the subdued and cautious coverage of the Japanese Cabinet changes in the Italian press.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Phillips reports Italian papers gave sparse, reserved coverage of the Japanese cabinet crisis, treating it as continued loyalty to the Tripartite Pact and barely mentioning Matsuoka.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1072 from Rome on Italian Press Reactions to the Japanese Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports Japanese press coverage highlighting Foreign Minister Toyoda's assurances to German and Italian ambassadors that foreign policy remains anchored in the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Tokyo papers stress the Tripartite Pact remains the foundation of policy; Toyoda assured the German and Italian ambassadors, and China policy remains focused on Nanking.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1053 from Tokyo on Diplomatic Assurances to Axis Ambassadors and Policy Toward China

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits an exchange of official messages between Prime Minister Konoye and Wang Ching-wei reaffirming Sino-Japanese collaboration.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Konoye and Wang Ching-wei exchanged messages: Konoye said policy toward Nanking is unaffected; Wang pledged cooperation for East Asian prosperity.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1062 from Tokyo on Exchange of Messages Between Premier Konoye and Wang Ching-wei

subfiles.about: Ambassador Steinhardt reports a confidential conversation with Japanese Ambassador Yoshitsugu Tatekawa regarding Indochina, Matsuoka's ouster, and the German military advance in Russia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Steinhardt reports Tatekawa attributed Matsuoka's ouster to personal jealousy, said Indochina move had Vichy's agreement, action against the USSR was on hold, and Germany would drive on Leningrad, Moscow and Kiev.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1402 from Moscow on Ambassador Tatekawa's Views on Japanese Moves and the Soviet Front

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports a Kokumin article discussing historical precedents for the military high command taking the initiative when government policy becomes stagnant.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports a Kokumin article: the military high command took the initiative after Manchurian and China incidents, and government must now act forcefully first to preserve unity.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1081 from Tokyo on Kokumin Article Regarding Government Policy and Military Initiative

subfiles.about: Consul Butrick reports political intelligence provided by Dr. J. Leighton Stuart concerning internal Japanese dissension, General Ugaki, and military disputes between Tojo and Itagaki.
subfiles.summary: Consul Butrick relays J. Leighton Stuart: Ugaki was considered for premier but liberals were too weak; Matsuoka was dropped for flexibility; Tojo and Itagaki quarreled over Itagaki's talks with Chiang. Stuart urges strong aid to China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 183 from Peiping transmitting Leighton Stuart's Insights on Japanese Leadership and Dissension

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the official appointment of Michiyo Iwamura as Minister of Justice in the third Konoye Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Michiyo Iwamura appointed Minister of Justice, relieving Konoye of that portfolio.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1086 from Tokyo announcing Appointment of Michiyo Iwamura as Justice Minister

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew relays a report from Consul Warner in Kobe detailing travel delays for British couriers, police surveillance of foreigners, and substantial Japanese naval movements in Bungo Strait.
subfiles.summary: Consul Warner at Kobe reports tightened security, Axis ships repainted gray, and a large Japanese naval force of 23 submarines, 3 cruisers and 2 carriers seen in Bungo Strait on July 21.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1069 from Tokyo transmitting Kobe Report on Courier Restrictions, Police Surveillance, and Naval Activity

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew comments on the Kokumin article as evidence that the military high command may have coerced the civilian government into the occupation of Indochina bases.
subfiles.summary: Grew considers the Kokumin article significant evidence the military high command may have forced the government's hand on occupying bases in French Indochina.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1090 from Tokyo on Military High Command Forcing Policy on French Indochina

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of State informs Ambassador Grew that intelligence indicates the move into Indochina was methodically planned with full cooperation between civilian and military authorities.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary replies that intelligence shows the Indochina advance was planned with full cooperation between the military and the civilian government, which had long favored it.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 441 to Tokyo regarding Government-Military Accord on Indochina Move

subfiles.about: FBI Director Hoover transmits a confidential intelligence memorandum describing hydroelectric dams, railway traffic, aircraft factories, and arsenals across the Japanese Empire.
subfiles.summary: FBI letter to Berle on installations in Japan, Korea and Manchuria: the Suiho Dam, Nagoya Mitsubishi plant with 60 German engineers, a Hokkaido tank arsenal, and Otaru fortifications.
subfiles.title: FBI Letter and Intelligence Memorandum on Industrial, Power, and Military Installations in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits Consul Warner's report from Kobe detailing dock entry pass restrictions on American President Lines personnel, heavy troop departures, and blocked Dutch funds.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards Consul Warner's Kobe report: dock pass refusals to American President Lines employees, heavy troop and freighter traffic, and ten million guilders in cotton goods blocked from export.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1119 and Paraphrase from Tokyo transmitting Kobe Report on Port Restrictions, Troop Shipments, and Blocked Funds

subfiles.about: State Department official Schmidt records a telephone inquiry from maritime attorney Paul H. Lacques regarding the specific dates the port of Kobe was closed to foreign shipping in the summer of 1941 prior to asset-freezing orders.
subfiles.summary: Schmidt records a call from lawyer Paul Lacques asking when Kobe port was closed to foreigners in 1941; Schmidt knew of periodic closures but not dates, and promised to check records.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Paul H. Lacques and Mr. Schmidt regarding Dates of Closure of the Port of Kobe
